text: The German Air Force, known in German as Luftwaffe (literally "air weapon," pronounced [ˈlʊftvafə]), is the aerial warfare branch of the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces. It was established in 1956 during the Cold War as part of the Bundeswehr, the armed forces of West Germany, following West Germany's accession to NATO in 1955. After German reunification in 1990, the Luftwaffe integrated elements of the former East German air force, the Luftstreitkräfte der NVA, which had been founded in 1956 as part of the National People's Army. There is no organizational continuity between the current Luftwaffe and the pre-1945 Wehrmacht Luftwaffe, which was disbanded in 1945/46 after World War II. The term Luftwaffe is used generically in German for any air force. The commander of the German Air Force is Lieutenant General Holger Neumann. As of 2015, the Luftwaffe operates from eleven air bases, two of which host no flying units, and maintains a presence at three civil airports. In 2012, it had an authorized strength of 28,475 active airmen and 4,914 reservists. After World War II, military aviation in Germany was banned by the Allied Control Commission, which disbanded the Nazi-era Luftwaffe in August 1946. The new Luftwaffe began operations in January 1956 with its first volunteers arriving at Nörvenich Air Base and receiving the US-made Republic F-84 Thunderstreak. Initially, it was divided into two operational commands: one in Northern Germany aligned with the British-led Second Allied Tactical Air Force and one in Southern Germany aligned with the American-led Fourth Allied Tactical Air Force. In 1957, the Luftwaffe took command of Army Air Defence Troops in Rendsburg and began expanding its air defense missile capabilities. The first operational unit was Air Transport Wing 61 at Erding Air Base, followed by the 31st Fighter-Bomber Squadron at Büchel Air Base. In 1958, the Luftwaffe received its first conscripts. In 1959, the 11th Missile Group in Kaufbeuren, armed with MGM-1 Matador surface-to-surface tactical nuclear cruise missiles, became operational. That same year, Fighter Wing 71 (Jagdgeschwader 71) equipped with Canadair CL-13 fighters became operational at Ahlhorner Heide Air Base. All aircraft, including current ones, feature the Iron Cross on the fuselage, a symbol from pre-March 1918, and the national flag of West Germany on the tail. In 1960, the Luftwaffe received its first Lockheed F-104 Starfighter jets, which remained in service until 1991. A total of 916 Starfighters were acquired, 292 of which crashed, resulting in 116 pilot deaths. This led to the Starfighter crisis in 1966, following 27 crashes and 17 casualties in 1965 alone. The West German public referred to the F-104 as the Witwenmacher (widow-maker), fliegender Sarg (flying coffin), Fallfighter (falling fighter), and Erdnagel (tent peg). On 25 August 1966, Defence Minister Kai-Uwe von Hassel relieved Chief Inspector Werner Panitzki and appointed Colonel Erich Hartmann, commander of the 71st Fighter Squadron, as Chief Inspector, due to public criticism of the Starfighter acquisition. On 2 September 1966, Johannes Steinhoff, with Günther Rall as deputy, became Chief Inspector. Steinhoff and Rall concluded that the non-German F-104s were safer and visited the US to study the aircraft, identifying deficiencies in training—such as lack of mountain and foggy-weather training and the aircraft's handling characteristics, including rapid, high-G turns—which contributed to accidents. They revised the training regimen, reducing accident rates to those comparable or better than other air forces and establishing a culture of high professionalism and tactical combat training outside Germany. Despite this, the F-104 retained its "widow-maker" reputation and was replaced earlier than in other nations by the McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II and the Panavia Tornado. On Steinhoff's initiative, the Luftwaffe established the German Air Force Command USA/Canada in Fort Bliss for missile and air defense training and pilot basic training, and a Tactical Training Command in Beja, Portugal, for Close Air Support training. Between 1967 and 1970, the Luftwaffe reorganized its forces, dissolving the two operational commands and dividing the four mixed Air Force divisions into two flying and two air defense divisions, with the remainder forming functional commands. Over the next decade, it received new equipment: in 1968, the first C-160 Transall transport planes; in 1974, the F-4 Phantom II fighter-bombers; in 1978, the first Alpha Jet Version A light attack jets; and in 1979, the first of 212 Panavia Tornado fighters. In 1986, the air defense forces began replacing Nike Hercules missiles with the MIM-104 Patriot and Roland short-range missile systems. Germany participates in NATO's nuclear sharing concept, allowing member nations without nuclear weapons to participate in nuclear weapon delivery. The Luftwaffe began training with the US Seventeenth Air Force in handling, arming, and delivering nuclear weapons. Initially, the F-104 was intended as a nuclear delivery platform with nuclear air-to-air and air-to-surface missiles and bombs. The Tornado became the second aircraft capable of delivering nuclear weapons, limited to B61 bombs. From 1965 to 1970, Missile Wings 1 and 2 operated 16 Pershing 1 missile systems with nuclear warheads under US Army custody, upgraded to Pershing 1a with 72 missiles in 1970. Although not directly affected by the 1988 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, the Luftwaffe removed the Pershing 1a missiles from its inventory in 1991 and destroyed them. At the end of the Cold War, over 100,000 soldiers served in the Luftwaffe. The United States continues to lend nuclear weapons for hypothetical use under the nuclear sharing agreement. In 2007, 22 B61 nuclear bombs were stored at Büchel Air Base for use with Tornado IDS fighter-bombers of Tactical Air Force Wing 33. American nuclear weapons previously stored at Nörvenich, Ramstein, and Memmingen were withdrawn during the mid- to late-1990s. By international treaties with the "Big Four" powers—United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, and France—East Germany was a nuclear-free zone; the latter three no longer have nuclear weapons in Germany. After reunification in October 1990, the aircraft and personnel of the former East German air force were integrated into the Luftwaffe. The remnants were placed under the newly formed 5th Air Force Division (5. Luftwaffendivision) in Strausberg, renamed in 1993 to the 3rd Air Force Division (3. Luftwaffendivision), moved to Gatow in Berlin, and assigned to NATO in 1995. By 1990, East German aircraft markings were replaced by the Air Force Iron Cross, marking the first time Soviet-built aircraft served in a NATO air force. However, due to incompatibility with Western NATO equipment, most of the East German aircraft—such as the Sukhoi Su-17, MiG-21, MiG-23, and MiG-29—were retired and sold or transferred to NATO members in Eastern Europe, including Poland and the Baltic states. An exception was Fighter Wing 3 "Vladimir Komarov" (Jagdfliegergeschwader 3 "Vladimir Komarov") at Preschen Air Base, which flew new MiG-29 fighters. On 1 June 1993, it was renamed Fighter Wing 73 (Jagdgeschwader 73) and moved to Laage Air Base on 1 October 1994. The pilots were among the world's most experienced MiG-29 operators and served as aggressor pilots for dissimilar combat training. The United States sent fighter pilots to Germany during the Red October exercise to practice tactics against MiG-29s. The MiG-29s were fully integrated into the Luftwaffe's air defense structure and became the first Soviet Bloc aircraft to be operationally deployed within NATO. With the introduction of the Eurofighter Typhoon, the decision was made to withdraw the MiG-29s. All MiG-29s, except one, were sold to Poland for €1 each. On 9 August 2004, the last MiG-29s arrived in Poland and continue to serve in the 41st Tactical Squadron of the Polish Air Force. The Luftwaffe experienced its first combat action since World War II in September 1995 during Operation Deliberate Force, when six IDS Tornado fighter-bombers, equipped with forward-looking infrared devices, and escorted by eight ECR Tornados, supported NATO artillery missions against Bosnian Serb positions near Sarajevo. In March 1999, during the Kosovo War, the Luftwaffe participated directly in combat with Fighter Bomber Wing 32, equipped with ECR Tornados, which conducted missions to suppress enemy air defenses in Kosovo. These aircraft were equipped with an electronic countermeasures pod, one AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile, and an AGM-88 HARM air-to-ground missile. The wing flew 2,108 hours and 446 sorties, firing 236 HARM missiles at hostile targets, with no manned aircraft lost. In 2005 and 2008, Luftwaffe F-4F Phantom II fighters participated in the Baltic Air Policing operation, supplemented in 2009 by Typhoon units. In 2006, the Luftwaffe deployed several Panavia Tornado reconnaissance planes from the 51st Reconnaissance Wing "Immelmann" stationed in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, and German Army helicopters also operated from the Luftwaffe air base there. Additionally, C-160 Transall transport aircraft conducted missions in and around Afghanistan. Since the 1970s, the West German and post-reunification German Luftwaffe, along with other European air forces, has pursued the development of European-made warplanes, including the Panavia Tornado and the Eurofighter Typhoon, introduced in 2006. On 13 January 2004, Minister of Defence Peter Struck announced plans to reduce the number of fighter planes from 426 in early 2004 to 265 by 2015. Assuming full implementation of the order for 180 Typhoons and the removal of all F-4 Phantoms, the number of Tornado fighter-bombers would be reduced to 85. Previously, the Bundesmarine's naval air wing (Marineflieger) operated 112 Tornado IDS aircraft; however, the last unit was disbanded in late 2004, and the entire maritime combat role was transferred to the Luftwaffe, with one unit equipped to carry Kormoran II and American HARM missiles. As of 2014, a significant portion of Germany's military aircraft was unserviceable, with approximately half of the Eurofighters and Tornados not airworthy, and the aging C-160 fleet operating in limited service while awaiting the introduction of the Airbus A400M, the first of which was delivered in December 2014. Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged that due to the poor state of Bundeswehr equipment, Germany could no longer fulfill its NATO commitments. The Luftwaffe was one of the founding members of the European Air Transport Command (EATC) headquartered in Eindhoven, Netherlands, and most of its transport and tanker assets are managed under EATC. In 2018, the replacement of four Airbus A310 MRTTs with Airbus A330 MRTTs was approved, with four units acquired by the Royal Netherlands Air Force. Future plans include replacing the aging Sikorsky CH-53 Sea Stallion, acquired in the 1970s, with Boeing CH-47 Chinook or Sikorsky CH-53K King Stallion. A bid for a heavy transport helicopter (STH) program was initiated in 2018 but suspended in 2020 due to high costs. The Luftwaffe also participated in the Israeli Air Force's "Blue Flag" exercise, the country's largest international air combat exercise, simulating extreme combat scenarios. The German Air Force contributed six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets from Tactical Air Force Squadron 73 Steinhoff based in Rostock.

The German Air Force is one of the founding members of the European Air Transport Command (EATC), headquartered in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, and most of its Transport & Tanker assets are now under EATC management. In 2018, the German Air Force approved the replacement of four Airbus A310 MRTT aircraft with four Airbus A330 MRTT aircraft, a decision made in conjunction with the Royal Netherlands Air Force. Future plans include replacing the aging Sikorsky CH-53 Sea Stallion, acquired in the 1970s, with either the Boeing CH-47 Chinook or the Sikorsky CH-53K King Stallion. A bid for a heavy transport helicopter program (STH) was initiated in 2018 but suspended in 2020 due to high costs. The Luftwaffe participated in the Israeli Air Force's "Blue Flag" exercise, the country's largest international air combat exercise, for the first time, with six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets from Tactical Air Force Squadron 73 Steinhoff based in Rostock. In 2018, the Air Force issued a request for information on four aircraft to replace the Panavia Tornado—Eurofighter Typhoon, F-15 Advanced Eagle, F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, and F-35 Lightning—before dropping the F-35 in January 2019, leaving the Eurofighter Typhoon and Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet as options. The German Air Force will acquire three C-130J Super Hercules transport and three KC-130J tanker aircraft, with deliveries planned for 2020–2021, jointly operated with the French Air Force’s two C-130J and two KC-130J aircraft (delivered 2018–19). In April 2020, the German government announced plans to purchase 30 F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, 15 EA-18G Growlers, and 55 Eurofighter Typhoons to replace the Tornado fleet, though approval was unlikely before 2022. The Super Hornet was selected for its compatibility with nuclear weapons and availability of an electronic attack variant, though as of March 2022, it had not been certified for the B61 Mod 12 nuclear bombs, with Boeing stating it believed it could meet German requirements with U.S. government support. In December 2021, Air Transport Wing 63 at Hohn Air Base, including the last remaining German C-160 Transalls, was disbanded, with the A400M and C-130J now serving as the primary tactical transport aircraft. In March 2022, Minister of Defence Christine Lambrecht announced Germany would buy 35 Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II fighter jets instead of Super Hornets, the only aircraft capable of carrying U.S. nuclear weapons, with an additional ten potentially added; Germany also planned to order 15 Eurofighter Typhoon electronic warfare aircraft to replace Growlers. In April 2022, Germany selected the CH-47F Chinook to replace its CH-53 Sea Stallion fleet as part of the STH program, with a contract worth approximately €5 billion (US$5.40 billion) for 60 aircraft. In August 2022, Germany deployed six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets, three Airbus A330 MRTT tankers, and four Airbus A400M Atlas transports to Exercise Pitch Black in Australia, its largest peacetime deployment. From 12 to 23 June 2023, the German Air Force hosted Air Defender 23, the largest NATO air exercise since its creation, involving 25 nations and up to 10,000 troops. The current commander of the German Air Force is Lieutenant General Holger Neumann. The Inspector of the Air Force (Inspekteur der Luftwaffe) is the commander of Air Force Command (Kommando Luftwaffe), established in 2013 through the merger of the Air Force Office, German Air Staff, and Air Force Forces Command. This command, similar to the U.S. Air Force Air Staff, is a force-providing command, not an operational one, responsible for ensuring combat readiness of combat units, which during operations are commanded by NATO or the Joint Operations Command of the Bundeswehr. The Air Force Command directly controls three higher commands. The creation of the Air Force Command was part of a 2011 Bundeswehr reorganization announced by Thomas de Maizière, which reduced the Air Force to 23,000 personnel and led to the disbanding of the three air divisions, Air Force Training Command, and Air Force Weapon Systems Command. The three surface-to-air missile units merged into a single wing at Husum, fielding 14 MIM-104 Patriot and 4 MANTIS systems. The three air transport wings were merged into a single wing at Wunstorf Air Base, fielding 40 A400M Atlas transport planes. The Luftwaffe will field three Multirole Eurofighter Wings, each with two squadrons for a total of 143 Eurofighter Typhoons. A fighter-bomber wing with Panavia Tornado IDS remains at Büchel Air Base, and Reconnaissance Wing 51 at Schleswig Air Base will retain its Tornado ECR squadron and add one drone squadron. The Kommando Luftwaffe has two main elements: individual units fall under the Air Force Operational Forces Command or Support Forces Command, and only come under Air Operations Command during deployment or EU/NATO attachments. In 2021, the Space Component Command (Weltraumkommando der Bundeswehr) was established. The main subordinate elements of the Air Operations Command, Air Force Operational Forces Command, and direct subordinated institutions are detailed in the document. The Air Force operates 12 air bases in 2020, four of which host no flying units, and has a presence at three civilian airports, including Berlin Tegel, which closed in November 2020. In 2012, the Air Force had an authorized strength of 44,565 active airmen/women and 4,914 reservists; civil personnel are being reduced to 5,950, mostly in maintenance and the Air Force Fire Department. On 20 September 2011, Defense Minister Thomas de Maizière announced the Air Force would shrink to 23,000 airmen/women. The Luftwaffe has five training institutions: Offizierschule der Luftwaffe, Unteroffizierschule der Luftwaffe, Luftwaffenausbildungsbataillon, Fachschule der Luftwaffe, and Technische Ausbildungszentrum der Luftwaffe. Originally, German Air Force aircraft featured an Iron Cross on all four wing positions and on both sides of the fuselage rear, with a small tricolor flag on the vertical stabilizer and a serial number of two letters (service and combat wing) followed by three numbers (squadron and aircraft number), resembling U.S. Air Force buzz numbers. This system was replaced in 1968 with a four-digit registration code, separated by an Iron Cross: the first two digits identify the aircraft type, the last two are sequential per type. For example, Tornado IDS are numbered 4301–4622, Tornado ECR 4623–4657, and Eurofighters 3001–3399; the format is often written with a "+" as a placeholder, e.g., "10+01" for the A350 fleet. Air Force ranks match those of the German Army, with the same field dress and dark blue dress uniform featuring gold-yellow winged collar patches; dark blue side or peaked caps are worn, and members of the German Air Force Regiment wear a dark blue beret. The rank insignia for commissioned officers and non-commissioned officers/enlisted personnel are as described. Germany participates in the MRTT program for aerial refueling and contracts Noordzee Helikopters Vlaanderen for H145 rotorcraft training. As of August 2025, Germany plans to invest €350 billion in new equipment through 2041, in addition to a special fund of €100 billion, covering specific budget allocations. Numerous books, magazines, and articles have been written about the Luftwaffe.
